contribution: The first quantum explanation of the course: the photoelectric effect shows where the classical wave model of light fails, introduces the photon $E = hf$, the work function and Einstein's equation $E_{\text{k,max}} = hf - W$, and prepares the measurement of Planck's constant at the Fotoni lab visit.
learn: explain the photoelectric effect with photons and the work function.
calculate the energy of a photon and the largest kinetic energy of the freed electrons.
determine Planck's constant from the slope of a stopping-voltage graph.
prior: Planck explained the radiation of hot objects with energy packets $E = hf$ (chapter *When classical physics ran out of answers*)
The frequency and wavelength of light are linked by $c = f\lambda$, and a charge $q$ moving through a voltage $U$ gains or loses the energy $qU$ (earlier physics courses)

activities.text: Imagine a clean metal plate inside a glass tube with no air in it. You shine a very bright red lamp on the plate. Nothing happens: no electrons leave the plate, even after many minutes. Then you switch on a weak violet lamp. Electrons fly out of the plate at once. Around 1900 almost every physicist believed that light is a wave, and a stronger wave carries more energy.
activities.question: How can weak light do something that strong light cannot?

activities.title: Review: Planck's energy packets
activities.prompt: In the chapter *When classical physics ran out of answers*, Planck explained the radiation of hot objects by assuming that energy is exchanged in packets of size $E = hf$. What does this mean for radiation of a higher frequency $f$?

choices.text: Each energy packet is larger.
choices.feedback: Right. $h$ is a constant, so the packet $hf$ grows in proportion to the frequency: doubling $f$ doubles the size of one packet. Today you will see what this means when light hits a metal.

choices.text: There are more packets every second, but each packet is the same size.
choices.feedback: The size of a packet is $hf$, so it changes with the frequency. The *number* of packets every second is a different thing: it depends on how much radiation there is.

choices.text: The packets become smaller, because high-frequency radiation has a short wavelength.
choices.feedback: A short wavelength means a *high* frequency ($c = f\lambda$), and $E = hf$ grows with $f$. Short-wavelength radiation, such as ultraviolet, has the larger packets.

activities.title: Prediction 1: brighter red light
activities.prompt: Red light of wavelength $650\ \text{nm}$ falls on a sodium plate, and no current flows. Now you turn the red lamp up to full intensity. What happens?

choices.text: Electrons start to leave the plate, because brighter light carries more energy.
choices.feedback: This is what the wave model predicts, and the experiment rejects it: at $650\ \text{nm}$ the current stayed at $0\ \text{nA}$ even at $100\ \%$ intensity. A red photon has only $1.91\ \text{eV}$, less than the work function of sodium, $2.36\ \text{eV}$, and more photons do not make one photon bigger.

choices.text: After a delay, when the electrons have collected enough energy, they start to leave.
choices.feedback: The model values show no current at $650\ \text{nm}$, however long you wait. An electron absorbs one photon at a time and loses that energy again as heat before another photon arrives, so the energy does not add up. Real experiments show no such delay either.

choices.text: Still no electrons leave the plate, however bright the red light is.
choices.feedback: The model values support this: at $650\ \text{nm}$ the current is $0\ \text{nA}$ even at full intensity, but at shorter wavelengths current flows. One red photon has $1.91\ \text{eV}$, less than the work function of sodium, $2.36\ \text{eV}$. More photons every second do not help, because each electron takes the energy of only one photon.

activities.title: Prediction 2: brighter violet light
activities.prompt: Violet light of wavelength $400\ \text{nm}$ frees electrons from sodium. You make the light three times as intense, from $30\ \%$ to $90\ \%$. What happens to the current $I$ and to the largest kinetic energy $E_{\text{k,max}}$ of the electrons?

choices.text: $I$ stays the same, but $E_{\text{k,max}}$ becomes three times as large.
choices.feedback: The model values show the opposite: $E_{\text{k,max}}$ stayed at $0.74\ \text{eV}$, but the current grew from $6.0\ \text{nA}$ to $18.0\ \text{nA}$. The energy of one photon, $3.10\ \text{eV}$, depends on the wavelength only.

choices.text: $I$ becomes three times as large, but $E_{\text{k,max}}$ stays the same.
choices.feedback: The model values support this: the current grew from $6.0\ \text{nA}$ to $18.0\ \text{nA}$, and $E_{\text{k,max}}$ stayed at $0.74\ \text{eV}$. Three times as many photons every second free three times as many electrons, but each photon still has $3.10\ \text{eV}$.

choices.text: Both become three times as large.
choices.feedback: Only the current grew, from $6.0\ \text{nA}$ to $18.0\ \text{nA}$. $E_{\text{k,max}} = hf - W$ contains no intensity: it stayed at $0.74\ \text{eV}$, because each electron still takes the energy of just one photon.

choices.text: Neither changes, because the colour of the light is the same.
choices.feedback: The colour fixes the energy of one photon, so $E_{\text{k,max}}$ stayed at $0.74\ \text{eV}$. But the current grew from $6.0\ \text{nA}$ to $18.0\ \text{nA}$: brighter light means more photons, and more photons free more electrons.

activities.text: A photocell: light falls on a metal plate in a vacuum tube. Change the wavelength, the intensity and the retarding voltage, and watch the electrons and the current.
activities.howto: *Wavelength* sets the colour of the light (below $380\ \text{nm}$ it is ultraviolet, drawn grey-violet). *Intensity* sets how many photons arrive every second. *Voltage* $U$ is the retarding voltage: it makes the collector negative, so it pushes the electrons back. Raise $U$ slowly until the ammeter shows $I = 0.0\ \text{nA}$: that is the stopping voltage $U_\text{s}$. The slider moves in steps of $0.02\ \text{V}$; after clicking it, the arrow keys move it one step at a time. *Metal* changes the work function. *Speed* changes only the animation.
activities.model: Each photon frees at most one electron, and only if $hf > W$. The work functions are typical textbook values (caesium $2.14\ \text{eV}$, potassium $2.29\ \text{eV}$, sodium $2.36\ \text{eV}$, zinc $4.3\ \text{eV}$); a real surface can differ by some tenths of an electronvolt. The freed electrons have kinetic energies spread evenly between $0$ and $E_{\text{k,max}}$. The current without a retarding voltage is proportional to the intensity and the same for every wavelength, a simplification. All readings are values of the model, not measurements.
activities.calc: $f = c/\lambda$ and $E = hf$ with $h = 6.62607015 \cdot 10^{-34}\ \text{J} \cdot \text{s}$ and $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$, shown in electronvolts. $E_{\text{k,max}} = hf - W$. With a retarding voltage $U$, only electrons with $E_\text{k} > eU$ reach the collector, so $I = I_0 \left(1 - \dfrac{eU}{E_{\text{k,max}}}\right)$ for $eU < E_{\text{k,max}}$ and $I = 0$ above, where $I_0 = 20\ \text{nA}$ at $100\ \%$ intensity. The current is zero from $U_\text{s} = E_{\text{k,max}}/e$ on.

activities.title: Experiment 1: colour and the stopping voltage
activities.intro: Test prediction 1, then measure the stopping voltage. The metal is sodium and the lamp is at full intensity. Start at $650\ \text{nm}$ and record the reading. Then choose shorter wavelengths, for example $500$, $450$, $400$, $350$ and $300\ \text{nm}$. At each one, raise the voltage $U$ slowly until the current is $I = 0.0\ \text{nA}$, and record. Keep your table: you need it for the conclusion.

activities.title: Experiment 2: brighter light
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. Violet light ($400\ \text{nm}$) falls on sodium, and there is no retarding voltage. Change only the intensity, for example $30\ \%$, $60\ \%$ and $90\ \%$, and record the current and the largest kinetic energy at each one.

activities.text:
Word bank

photon · photon energy $hf$ · work function $W$ · threshold frequency · intensity · current $I$ · stopping voltage $U_\text{s}$ · largest kinetic energy $E_{\text{k,max}}$ · to free (an electron) · to absorb · to depend on · to be independent of · proportional to

Sentence starters

  • The evidence suggests that …
  • When we increased the intensity, …
  • At a wavelength of … nm, the current stopped at …
  • This does not depend on …, but it does depend on …
  • The wave model predicts …, whereas the photon model …
  • I agree / I disagree with you, because …

activities.title: Conclusion: what frees the electrons?
activities.pair: Pair work: one of you explains aloud with the sentence starters, the other asks questions; then each of you writes your own answer.
activities.prompt: Discuss with a partner, then write four or five sentences. Use the numbers in your two tables. What decides *whether* electrons leave the sodium plate? What does a brighter lamp change, and what does it not change? How did the stopping voltage change when the wavelength became shorter?
activities.model: The evidence suggests that the colour of the light, not its brightness, decides whether electrons leave. At $650\ \text{nm}$ the current was $0\ \text{nA}$ even at full intensity, but at $500\ \text{nm}$ and shorter wavelengths current flowed. When we made violet light three times as intense, the current grew from $6.0\ \text{nA}$ to $18.0\ \text{nA}$, but the largest kinetic energy stayed at $0.74\ \text{eV}$. When the wavelength became shorter, the stopping voltage grew, for example from about $0.40\ \text{V}$ at $450\ \text{nm}$ to about $1.78\ \text{V}$ at $300\ \text{nm}$. So a higher frequency gives each electron more energy, and a brighter lamp only frees more electrons. These are values of a model, not measurements.
criteria: The answer says that below a certain frequency (above a certain wavelength) no electrons leave, whatever the intensity, with a value from the table.
The answer says that a higher intensity gives a larger current but the same largest kinetic energy, with numbers.
The answer says that the stopping voltage grows when the frequency grows (the wavelength gets shorter).
The answer uses at least three words from the word bank correctly and says the values come from a model.

activities.title: Words of the lesson
activities.text: Check the key words before you read about the people behind the equation.

activities.title: Read and compare: three roles in one discovery
activities.pair: Pair work: each of you reads one or two biographies and tells your partner about them.
activities.prompt: Read the three short biographies. Discuss with a partner, then write three sentences: one about Planck, one about Einstein and one about Millikan. Say what each one *did* for the photoelectric equation (proposed an idea, explained, tested). Which of them believed the photon idea at first?
activities.model: Planck introduced the energy packets $hf$ in 1900 to explain the radiation of hot objects, but he thought of them as a mathematical step and at first rejected light quanta. Einstein proposed in 1905 that light itself consists of quanta and used this idea to explain the photoelectric effect with the equation $E_{\text{k,max}} = hf - W$. Millikan tested the equation for about ten years and confirmed it in 1914–1916, although he did not believe in light quanta; he also measured $h$ from the slope. Only Einstein believed the photon idea at first.
criteria: The answer gives each person a different role: Planck an idea about energy packets, Einstein the photon explanation, Millikan the experimental test.
The answer says that Planck and Millikan both doubted light quanta at first.
Each sentence has a verb of action in the past tense (introduced, proposed, tested, confirmed).

activities.title: Back to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with your tables and with the photon model. Then answer the opening question in one or two sentences: why can a dim violet lamp free electrons when a bright red lamp cannot?

activities.title: Planck's constant from example data
activities.text:
A group measured the stopping voltage of a photocell with the spectral lines of a mercury lamp, like the measurement at Fotoni. The numbers below are an invented example, rounded like real readings.

| Wavelength $\lambda$ (nm) | Frequency $f$ ($10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$) | Stopping voltage $U_\text{s}$ (V) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 578.0 | 5.19 | 0.25 |
| **546.1** | **5.49** | **0.37** |
| 435.8 | 6.88 | 0.94 |
| 404.7 | 7.41 | 1.17 |
| **365.0** | **8.21** | **1.49** |

question.prompt: Use the two rows in bold. Calculate Planck's constant $h$ from the slope of the line $U_\text{s} = \dfrac{h}{e}\,f - \dfrac{W}{e}$. Give $h$ as a number times $10^{-34}\ \text{J} \cdot \text{s}$: for example, type $6.1$ for $6.1 \cdot 10^{-34}\ \text{J} \cdot \text{s}$.
hints: The slope of the line is $\Delta U_\text{s} / \Delta f$. Which two values of $U_\text{s}$ and $f$ do you need?
The slope is $h/e$, so $h = e \cdot \dfrac{\Delta U_\text{s}}{\Delta f}$, with $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$.

mistakes.feedback: You found the slope $\Delta U_\text{s}/\Delta f = 4.12 \cdot 10^{-15}\ \text{V} \cdot \text{s}$. That is $h/e$, not $h$: multiply it by $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$.
You used only one point, $h = eU_\text{s}/f$. That forgets the work function: $eU_\text{s} = hf - W$. Use the *difference* of two points, so that $W$ cancels.

question.solution:
**Given:** from the example table, $f_1 = 5.49 \cdot 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$, $U_1 = 0.37\ \text{V}$ and $f_2 = 8.21 \cdot 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$, $U_2 = 1.49\ \text{V}$; elementary charge $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$

**Find:** Planck's constant $h$ in $\text{J} \cdot \text{s}$

**Principle:** Einstein's equation with the stopping voltage, $eU_\text{s} = hf - W$, gives a straight line $U_\text{s} = \dfrac{h}{e}f - \dfrac{W}{e}$. Its slope is $h/e$. Taking the difference of two points removes the unknown work function $W$.

**Formula:** $eU_2 - eU_1 = hf_2 - hf_1$, from which

$$h = \frac{e\,(U_2 - U_1)}{f_2 - f_1}$$

**Conversions:** None are needed: volts times coulombs give joules, and $\text{J}/\text{Hz} = \text{J} \cdot \text{s}$. The frequencies are written out with the power of ten.

**Substitution:** $h = \dfrac{1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{C} \cdot (1.49\ \text{V} - 0.37\ \text{V})}{(8.21 - 5.49) \cdot 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}} = \dfrac{1.794 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{J}}{2.72 \cdot 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}} = 6.597 \cdot 10^{-34}\ \text{J} \cdot \text{s}$

**Answer:** $h \approx 6.60 \cdot 10^{-34}\ \text{J} \cdot \text{s}$, three significant figures, as in the differences $1.12\ \text{V}$ and $2.72 \cdot 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$.

**Reasonableness:** The exact value is $6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\ \text{J} \cdot \text{s}$, so the result is about $0.4\ \%$ too small, which is well within the reading precision of $0.01\ \text{V}$: an error of $0.01\ \text{V}$ in $\Delta U_\text{s}$ changes $h$ by almost $1\ \%$. Using two points far apart, as here, keeps this error small.

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt:
Light of wavelength $500\ \text{nm}$ falls on caesium, $W = 2.14\ \text{eV}$. A student writes:

$$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = 3.97 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$$

$$\begin{aligned} E_{\text{k,max}} &= E - W \\ &= 3.97 - 2.14 = 1.83\ \text{eV} \end{aligned}$$

Where is the error?

choices.text: The photon energy is in joules and the work function in electronvolts: $E = 3.97 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{J} = 2.48\ \text{eV}$, so $E_{\text{k,max}} = 0.34\ \text{eV}$.
choices.feedback: Right. The student subtracted numbers in two different units. Convert first: $3.97 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{J} : 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{J/eV} = 2.48\ \text{eV}$, then $2.48\ \text{eV} - 2.14\ \text{eV} = 0.34\ \text{eV}$.

choices.text: The work function should be added: $E_{\text{k,max}} = E + W$.
choices.feedback: Energy is conserved: the photon's energy is *shared* between the work function and the kinetic energy, $hf = W + E_{\text{k,max}}$. So $W$ is subtracted. The real error is in the units.

choices.text: The wavelength should be in nanometres in $hc/\lambda$, which gives a different photon energy.
choices.feedback: With $\lambda = 5.00 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}$ in SI units, $hc/\lambda = 3.97 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ is right. The error comes in the next line, where joules and electronvolts are mixed.

choices.text: There is no error in the calculation.
choices.feedback: Look at the units in the subtraction: $3.97$ is in units of $10^{-19}\ \text{J}$, but $2.14$ is in electronvolts. The answer $1.83\ \text{eV}$ is about five times too large.

activities.title: 1. Concept: brightness or colour?
activities.prompt: Zinc has a work function of about $4.3\ \text{eV}$. One zinc plate is lit by a very bright green lamp ($530\ \text{nm}$, photon energy $2.34\ \text{eV}$) for an hour. Another zinc plate is lit for one second by a dim ultraviolet lamp ($250\ \text{nm}$, photon energy $4.96\ \text{eV}$). Which plate gives off electrons?

choices.text: Only the plate under the dim ultraviolet lamp, and the electrons leave at once.
choices.feedback: Right. One ultraviolet photon, $4.96\ \text{eV}$, is more than the work function, so it can free an electron immediately. A green photon, $2.34\ \text{eV}$, is too small, and a brighter lamp or a longer time only gives more photons that are too small.

choices.text: Only the plate under the bright green lamp, because it receives far more energy in an hour.
choices.feedback: The total energy is large, but it arrives in packets of $2.34\ \text{eV}$, and each electron takes only one packet. Since $2.34\ \text{eV} < 4.3\ \text{eV}$, no electron can leave. This was exactly the wave model's mistake.

choices.text: Both plates, the green one after a delay while the energy builds up.
choices.feedback: An electron does not store the energy of many photons: the energy turns into heat in the metal before the next photon arrives. There is no delay that helps, and green light never frees electrons from zinc.

choices.text: Neither plate, because the ultraviolet lamp is too dim.
choices.feedback: A dim lamp sends fewer photons, but each ultraviolet photon still has $4.96\ \text{eV}$, more than $4.3\ \text{eV}$. So a few electrons leave: the current is small, not zero.

activities.title: 2. Calculation: the stopping voltage
activities.prompt: Light with a photon energy of $3.10\ \text{eV}$ ($400\ \text{nm}$) falls on sodium, $W = 2.36\ \text{eV}$. What is the stopping voltage $U_\text{s}$?

choices.feedback: This is the photon energy divided by $e$. But the electron first uses $2.36\ \text{eV}$ to escape: $eU_\text{s} = hf - W$.
You added the work function. The photon's energy is shared: $hf = W + E_{\text{k,max}}$, so $E_{\text{k,max}} = 3.10\ \text{eV} - 2.36\ \text{eV}$.

Right. $E_{\text{k,max}} = 3.10\ \text{eV} - 2.36\ \text{eV} = 0.74\ \text{eV}$, and $eU_\text{s} = E_{\text{k,max}}$ gives $U_\text{s} = 0.74\ \text{V}$. An energy in electronvolts and the voltage in volts have the same number for one electron.
$1.19 \cdot 10^{-19}$ is $E_{\text{k,max}}$ in *joules*. The voltage is $U_\text{s} = E_{\text{k,max}}/e = 1.19 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{J} : 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\ \text{C} = 0.74\ \text{V}$.

activities.title: 3. Graph: two metals
activities.prompt: Students measure the stopping voltage $U_\text{s}$ at several frequencies $f$ for caesium ($W = 2.14\ \text{eV}$) and for zinc ($W = 4.3\ \text{eV}$), and draw both graphs in one coordinate system. How do the two lines compare?

choices.text: The zinc line is steeper, because zinc has the larger work function.
choices.feedback: The slope of $U_\text{s} = \dfrac{h}{e}f - \dfrac{W}{e}$ is $h/e$, which contains no property of the metal. The work function only moves the line along the frequency axis.

choices.text: They are the same line, because $h$ is the same for every metal.
choices.feedback: The slopes are the same, but $W$ is different, so the lines start at different threshold frequencies $f_0 = W/h$: caesium at about $5.2 \cdot 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$, zinc at about $10.4 \cdot 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$.

choices.text: They are parallel; the zinc line starts at a higher frequency on the $f$ axis.
choices.feedback: Right. Both lines have the slope $h/e$. Zinc needs more energy, so its threshold frequency $f_0 = W/h \approx 10.4 \cdot 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$ is higher than that of caesium, $5.2 \cdot 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$, and its line lies to the right.

choices.text: The caesium line is steeper, because caesium releases more electrons.
choices.feedback: The number of electrons changes the *current*, not the stopping voltage. The slope of every $U_\text{s}$–$f$ line is $h/e$.

activities.title: 4. Explain and argue
activities.prompt: Your friend says: "If we only had a powerful enough red laser, it would knock electrons out of zinc." Do you agree? Explain with the photon model and a calculation or a number, and suggest what light would work instead.
activities.model: I disagree. Red light of about $650\ \text{nm}$ has photons of $hf = hc/\lambda \approx 1.9\ \text{eV}$, but the work function of zinc is about $4.3\ \text{eV}$. Each electron absorbs only one photon, so a more powerful laser only sends more photons that are each too small: the current stays zero. Light works only if $hf > W$, so the wavelength must be shorter than $hc/W \approx 290\ \text{nm}$. Ultraviolet light, even a dim lamp, would free electrons from zinc.
criteria: The answer compares the energy of one red photon (about $1.9\ \text{eV}$) with the work function of zinc (about $4.3\ \text{eV}$).
The answer explains that a more powerful laser means more photons, not bigger ones, and that one electron takes one photon.
The answer suggests ultraviolet light, ideally with the threshold wavelength (about $290\ \text{nm}$) or frequency.
The answer takes a clear position (agree or disagree) and gives a reason.

activities.text:
Le coin français

Physics is the same in every language. In French, the photoelectric effect is l'effet photoélectrique, and Einstein's idea is that la lumière is made of photons. Listen, repeat, and then say the last sentence to your partner.
